query: In conventional alloys, loss of toughness has long been associated with grain-boundary segregation and brittle grain-boundary precipitation. By contrast, compositionally complex high-entropy alloys can suppress rapid grain coarsening and deleterious intermetallic formation and have shown favorable strength–ductility combinations and resistance to high-temperature softening and low-temperature embrittlement. These findings do not establish what governs possible toughness degradation in an initially single-phase high-entropy alloy. Under the constraint of retaining a compositionally complex alloy suitable for demanding engineering service, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains whether and why brittle behavior emerges? Specify a controlled comparison that would distinguish the hypothesis from conventional-alloy expectations, predicted observations relative to the initial baseline, its service and loading boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification outcome.

generation.hypothesis: In a single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy, slow-cooling during controlled isothermal aging promotes nanoclustering of principal elements (Cr, Ni, and Mn) at grain boundaries, which reduces grain-boundary cohesion and leads to earlier intergranular cracking (i.e., a loss of toughness), compared to a rapidly quenched, compositionally homogeneous state.
generation.material_initial_state: A single-phase face-centered cubic CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy produced via arc melting and homogenized to ensure uniform composition and microstructure.
generation.intervention: Perform an isothermal aging study at intermediate temperatures (400–600°C) with two processing routes: one with rapid quenching to freeze the homogeneous state and one with slow cooling to promote grain-boundary nanoclustering.
generation.conditions: Identical aging durations at 400–600°C followed by tensile testing at room temperature and moderately elevated temperatures; specimens will be processed under the same homogenization treatments to isolate cooling rate effects.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of nanoclusters enriched in Cr, Ni, and Mn at grain boundaries in the slowly cooled samples, as compared to the minimal clustering in rapidly quenched samples.
generation.mechanism: Nanoclustering at grain boundaries reduces local cohesion by concentrating specific alloying elements, thereby lowering the resistance to intergranular crack initiation under mechanical load. This mechanism for toughness degradation is distinct from the brittle phase precipitation seen in conventional alloys.
generation.predicted_outcome: Slow-cooled samples are expected to show a significant reduction in toughness, evidenced by lower crack initiation strain and an increased prevalence of intergranular fracture modes relative to rapidly quenched samples. In contrast, rapidly quenched specimens should maintain higher toughness due to more homogeneous grain-boundary chemistry.
generation.baseline: The rapidly quenched, compositionally homogeneous CrMnFeCoNi alloy exhibiting minimal nanoclustering at grain boundaries and superior toughness.
generation.boundary: This mechanism is anticipated to be prominent under intermediate aging temperatures (400–600°C) and may not be the dominant factor at temperatures where nanoclusters are unstable (e.g., above 800°C) or under loading conditions with drastically different strain rates.
generation.uncertainty: Quantitative effects on toughness degradation depend on the precise kinetics of nanoclustering, and potential overlap with early precipitation phenomena; high-resolution characterization is required to definitively isolate the effect.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of CrMnFeCoNi HEA specimens: one set aged at 400–600°C followed by rapid quenching, and a second set aged under the same conditions with slow cooling. Conduct identical tensile tests on both specimen sets at room and moderately elevated temperatures.
measurements: Atom probe tomography (APT) or high-resolution TEM to quantify grain-boundary nanoclustering of Cr, Ni, and Mn.
Mechanical testing to measure crack initiation strain, fracture toughness, and determine fracture mode (intergranular vs transgranular).
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If both sets of specimens (rapidly quenched and slow-cooled) exhibit statistically equivalent grain-boundary chemistry and similar mechanical toughness (including crack initiation strain and fracture mode), then the hypothesis that nanoclustering is the controlling factor for toughness degradation would be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs reduces GB cohesion in single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloys. AbstractThe loss of ductility with temperature has been widely observed in tensile tests of single-phase face-centered cubic structured high-entropy alloys (HEAs). However, the fundamental mechanism for such a ductility loss remains unknown. Here, we show that ductility loss in the CrMnFeCoNi HEA upon deformation at intermediate temperatures is correlated with cracking at grain boundaries (GBs). Nanoclustering Cr, Ni, and Mn separately at GBs, as detected by atom probe tomography, reduces GB cohesion and promotes crack initiation along GBs. We further demonstrated a GB segregation engineering strategy to avoid ductility loss by shifting the fast segregation of principal elements from GBs into preexisting Cr-rich secondary phases. We believe that GB decohesion by nanoclustering multiprincipal elements is a common phenomenon in HEAs. This study not only provides insights into understanding ductility loss but also offers a strategy for tailoring ductility-temperature relations in HEAs.

In addition, the segregation of trace elements C and B into GBs is beneficial to improve GB cohesion as long as M6C carbides do not precipitate (, ). The 1D compositional profiles in fig. S4 show that the C and B composition at Cr-enriched and Ni(Mn)-enriched GBs is very low, which is insufficient to form carbides or borides at GBs. A recent study of the single-phase fcc CoFeNi2V0.5Mo0.2 HEA demonstrated that the lack of Cr and Mn can evade ductility loss at intermediate temperatures (). Therefore, we believe that the segregation of Cr, Ni, and Mn at GBs in Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni system HEAs can embrittle GBs and, hence, lead to ductility loss with increasing deformation temperature. Note that the segregation of Cr, Ni, and Mn at GBs also occurs at relatively low temperatures (<700°C), which accounts for ductility loss at intermediate temperatures. In the current work, the sample after tensile test at 700°C, exhibiting remarkable ductility loss though maintaining a strain hardening capacity, provides a good model example to demonstrate our hypothesis: Nanoclustering induced GB embrittlement in HEAs at intermediate temperatures. It has been shown that Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni system HEAs exhibit an increased ductility and even superplasticity at temperatures over 900°C ().

We revealed the key mechanism responsible for the loss of the ductility with increasing temperature, a phenomenon widely reported in the single-phase fcc HEAs that are composed of three or more elements of Al, Cr, Mn, Fe, Co, and Ni. SEM of tensioned sample surfaces of single-phase coarse-grained Cr20Mn20Fe20Co20Ni20 HEA (grain size around 50 μm) suggested that ductility loss is correlated with the intergranular cracking. However, TEM along GBs confirmed that there are no precipitates of secondary phases along GBs. On the basis of APT analysis, we explored that ductility loss is attributed to fast nanosegregation of principal elements Ni, Cr, and Mn separately into GBs, which reduce GB cohesion and promote crack initiation along GBs. We further demonstrated a GB segregation engineering strategy to evade ductility loss by migrating fast segregation of the principal elements from GBs into preexisting Cr-rich secondary phases in an example HEA, i.e., Cr26Mn20Fe20Co20Ni14. Our work not only provides insights into understanding ductility loss but also offers a GB segregation engineering strategy of tailoring strength-ductility-temperature relations in HEAs.

proposals.intervention: Perform a controlled isothermal aging study with two sets: one with rapid quenching to freeze the homogeneous state and one with slow cooling to promote grain-boundary segregation and nanocluster formation
proposals.conditions: Aging at intermediate temperatures (e.g., 400–600°C) for varying durations followed by tensile testing at service-relevant temperatures (e.g., room and moderate elevated temperatures)
proposals.structural_mediator: Formation vs. absence of nanoclusters of key elements (Cr, Ni, Mn) at grain boundaries
proposals.mechanism: In contrast to conventional alloys where brittle phases appear via precipitation, slow cooling in HEAs can trigger diffusion‐controlled nanoclustering at grain boundaries. These clusters reduce local cohesion, facilitating intergranular crack initiation under load
proposals.predicted_outcome: Samples aged with slow cooling show reduced toughness and premature intergranular cracking relative to rapidly quenched, compositionally homogeneous samples. The brittle behavior should be evident only in the pre-aged, segregated samples, thereby distinguishing the HEA’s mechanism from conventional grain-boundary precipitation
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach directly tests whether grain-boundary nanoclustering governs toughness degradation in an initially single-phase HEA, providing a controlled comparison that isolates the effect of segregation from conventional precipitate-driven brittleness

proposals.intervention: Implement solution heat treatments at different cooling rates to modify grain-boundary morphology, producing straight versus serrated boundaries
proposals.conditions: Solution treatment at high temperatures with controlled cooling rates (e.g., fast quench vs. slow cooling) followed by tensile and creep testing at elevated service temperatures (around 650°C)
proposals.structural_mediator: Grain-boundary morphology (straight vs. serrated) that affects local strain distribution and potential sites for brittle failure
proposals.mechanism: Serrated boundaries, as opposed to straight ones, are hypothesized to disperse stress more effectively and impede localized decohesion. If brittle behavior emerges despite serration, it would implicate a different inherent segregation or precipitation mechanism in HEAs
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline with straight grain boundaries, the serrated boundary samples should demonstrate higher tensile fracture strains and longer creep rupture life, indicating improved toughness. A decisive falsification would occur if no significant toughness difference is observed, undermining the boundary morphology hypothesis
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This candidate distinguishes the HEA’s toughening mechanism from conventional alloys by showing that even in a compositionally complex system, grain-boundary architecture plays a critical role. It also defines clear service boundaries (650°C tensile and creep conditions) and provides a controlled comparison between two boundary morphologies

proposals.material_system: AlCoCrFeNi-based high-entropy alloy vs. AlCoCrFeNiMo0.25 variant
proposals.intervention: Introduce a minor alloying addition (Mo, ~5 at.%) while keeping the overall compositional complexity intact, and compare both variants under identical processing
proposals.conditions: Arc-melted ingots processed by identical homogenization treatments and tensile testing at room and elevated temperatures, in corrosive and mechanical loading environments
proposals.structural_mediator: Changes in grain boundary chemical bonding and possible suppression or promotion of brittle intermetallic formation
proposals.mechanism: The hypothesis is that Mo addition alters the local bonding at grain boundaries, potentially mitigating deleterious nanoclustering or unwanted interfacial phases that would promote brittle behavior. This contrasts with conventional alloys where alloying typically forms brittle intermetallics, but in HEAs the complex matrix may allow for improved cohesion
proposals.predicted_outcome: The Mo-alloyed HEA is expected to exhibit enhanced toughness and delayed onset of brittle intergranular fracture relative to the baseline composition. A decisive falsification would occur if both alloys display similar toughness degradation trends under identical conditions
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This proposal tests a compositional lever to modify interfacial chemistry without losing the intrinsic complexity of HEAs. It examines whether intrinsic bonding modifications at the grain boundaries can suppress the emergence of brittleness, directly contrasting with conventional alloy mechanisms

proposals.intervention: Perform pre-aging treatments at moderate temperatures to induce potential grain-boundary segregation, followed by dynamic mechanical testing at varied strain rates
proposals.conditions: Pre-aging at ~600°C for different durations to promote subtle grain boundary composition changes, then performing tensile tests across a range of strain rates (10^−3 to 10^3 s^−1) at service-relevant temperatures (including cryogenic and intermediate temperatures)
proposals.structural_mediator: Evolution of grain-boundary chemistry (segregation) and twin formation under dynamic loading
proposals.mechanism: It is hypothesized that pre-aging promotes segregation at grain boundaries in an otherwise single-phase alloy, which under dynamic loading conditions lowers grain-boundary cohesion. The competition between deformation-induced twinning and adiabatic heating could reveal a transition to brittle behavior if grain-boundary segregation dominates
proposals.predicted_outcome: Pre-aged samples are anticipated to show a lower onset strain for intergranular cracking and compromised toughness under high strain-rate conditions relative to unaged samples. A decisive falsification would be if pre-aging does not change the strain regime of crack initiation, indicating that mechanisms other than segregation control toughness
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By combining thermal pre-aging with dynamic mechanical testing, this experiment decouples the effects of grain-boundary segregation from deformation kinetics. It establishes service boundaries (high strain rates and varying temperature conditions) and provides a controlled comparison to discern if subtle compositional changes trigger brittle behavior in HEAs

critiques.addresses_problem: The proposal directly targets the origin of toughness degradation by focusing on grain‐boundary bonding alterations via Mo addition, thus addressing the question of why brittleness might emerge in an initially single‐phase HEA.
critiques.constraints: It satisfies the constraint of retaining compositional complexity using the AlCoCrFeNi system and only a minor modification; however, there is a risk of inadvertently stabilizing unwanted intermetallic phases within the same compositional framework.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism—altering local grain-boundary bonding to mitigate deleterious nanoclustering—is physically plausible but must contend with the possibility that Mo could also promote brittle σ phase formation as observed in similar systems.
critiques.feasibility: The approach is feasible with established methods (arc melting, homogenization, tensile testing) and is comparable to similar previous studies.
critiques.evidence: The proposed strategy is supported by studies such as PMC12525669 and PMC9572892, which demonstrate Mo’s effect on microstructure and mechanical properties. However, formation of brittle secondary phases may complicate the interpretation.
critiques.main_risk: The main risk is that the Mo addition might trigger the formation of brittle intermetallic (e.g., σ phase) that could compromise toughness instead of improving it.
critiques.fix: Incorporate phase characterization (e.g., XRD, TEM) to carefully optimize the Mo concentration and confirm that deleterious intermetallic phases are not forming.

critiques.addresses_problem: This direction directly probes whether grain‐boundary nanoclustering governs toughness degradation in a single‐phase HEA by comparing differences induced by quenching versus slow cooling.
critiques.constraints: It respects the constraints by operating within the CrMnFeCoNi system and using temperature regimes relevant to service conditions, and directly contrasts with conventional alloy behavior.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism—reduction of grain‐boundary cohesion by localized element clustering—is well supported by prior atom probe studies and is physically sound for HEAs.
critiques.feasibility: The experimental design involving controlled isothermal aging, cooling rate variations, and subsequent tensile testing is well within the scope of established techniques.
critiques.evidence: Multiple pieces of evidence from PMC6897545 (abstract, conclusions, and associated records) strongly support nanoclustering as a mechanism for grain‐boundary embrittlement.
critiques.main_risk: Accurately isolating the effect of nanoclustering from early-stage precipitation may be challenging during aging experiments.
critiques.fix: Employ high-resolution characterization techniques (e.g., atom probe tomography) to clearly differentiate nanoclustering from conventional precipitation.

critiques.addresses_problem: This direction investigates whether variations in grain‐boundary morphology (serrated vs. straight) are responsible for differences in toughness, thereby addressing a potential mechanism for brittleness that is distinct from conventional intermetallic precipitation.
critiques.constraints: It adheres to the constraint of maintaining a compositionally complex HEA (Al0.3CoCrFeNi) and sets service conditions (650°C tensile and creep testing) appropriately.
critiques.physical_soundness: The hypothesis that serrated boundaries distribute strain more evenly and impede localized decohesion is physically sound and supported by molecular dynamics simulations and prior experimental evidence.
critiques.feasibility: Solution heat treatment with controlled cooling rates is a standard processing method, and the subsequent mechanical testing is readily achievable with current experimental setups.
critiques.evidence: Evidence from PMC9848264 supports the effect of grain-boundary serration on improved tensile and creep properties, indicating that morphology influences ductility.
critiques.main_risk: There is a risk that differences in toughness could also arise from subtle compositional segregation effects at the grain boundaries rather than solely from morphological differences.
critiques.fix: Supplement grain-boundary morphology studies with detailed microchemical analyses (e.g., EDS or APT) to ensure that observed toughness differences are predominantly due to boundary shape.

critiques.addresses_problem: This proposal aims to uncover if grain‐boundary segregation induced by pre-aging can lead to brittle behavior under dynamic loading, thus addressing the mechanistic origin of toughness degradation in HEAs.
critiques.constraints: It complies with the requirement by using a compositionally complex, refractory BCC-phase HEA (NbTaTiV) and tests under varied strain rates and temperatures that mimic challenging service conditions.
critiques.physical_soundness: The mechanism—pre-aging induced segregation lowering grain-boundary cohesion under high strain rates—is conceptually sound, though it competes with deformation mechanisms like twinning and adiabatic heating.
critiques.feasibility: While the pre-aging and dynamic mechanical testing are within current experimental capabilities, decoupling the effect of segregation from competing high strain-rate phenomena can be challenging.
critiques.evidence: Evidence from PMC12463061 and related records shows dynamic deformation behavior in refractory HEAs; however, these studies primarily focus on strain hardening and have not decisively isolated segregation effects on toughness.
critiques.main_risk: The interplay between grain-boundary segregation and other dynamic deformation mechanisms (e.g., twinning, adiabatic heating) may obscure the direct impact on toughness.
critiques.fix: Incorporate in-depth post-mortem microstructural analyses to isolate segregation effects, possibly by testing over a narrower strain-rate regime where competing mechanisms are minimized.

decision.rationale: Direction B was chosen because it directly tests whether grain‐boundary nanoclustering governs toughness degradation in an initially single‐phase HEA. It offers a controlled comparison between rapidly quenched and slowly cooled conditions, which isolates the effect of nanoclustering from conventional precipitation mechanisms. This direction is supported by multiple pieces of prior evidence (e.g., PMC6897545::web::000::abstract, PMC6897545::web::008::nanoclustering_induced_gb_embrittlement, PMC6897545::web::009::nanoclustering_induced_gb_embrittlement, PMC6897545::web::013::conclusion) and does not require major modifications.
